platforms.title: A Sudden Shower of Eye Floaters Could Signal a Retinal Tear
platforms.meta_description: A few floaters drifting across your vision are usually fine, but a sudden burst with flashes can be different. Why same-day care matters for a retinal tear.
platforms.body_html:
Ever noticed thread-like specks drifting across your vision? Most of the time that's completely harmless, but the American Academy of Ophthalmology warns that a sudden burst of new floaters combined with flashes of light can mean something entirely different. That combination can signal a retinal tear — a genuine eye emergency.

Why floaters appear, and why they can suddenly increase

The eye is filled with a clear gel called the vitreous, and as people age, that gel gradually shrinks and becomes more watery. Clumps of collagen fibers inside it cast tiny shadows onto the retina, which is what shows up as floaters — mostly a harmless part of getting older on its own. But as the shrinking vitreous pulls away from the retina, it occasionally tugs hard enough to actually tear it. If fluid seeps through that tear, it can lift the retina away entirely — retinal detachment, which can cause permanent vision loss.

According to the American Academy of Ophthalmology, the biggest risk factors are being over 50, severe nearsightedness, previous eye surgery like cataract surgery, a retinal detachment in the other eye, eye trauma, and family history. Any of these make it easier for the vitreous to tear the retina as it pulls away.

How to tell ordinary floaters apart from an emergency

First, a handful of floaters that stay roughly the same in number over time. That's usually nothing to worry about — just an ordinary part of the eye aging.

Second, a sudden burst of many new floaters, flashes of light like a camera flash off to the side of your vision, or a curtain or shadow spreading across part of your sight. That's not something to watch for a few days — it calls for same-day eye care.

If those warning signs show up, an eye doctor will dilate the pupil to examine the retina directly. If a tear is caught early, laser treatment can seal it off before it progresses to a full detachment. If the retina has already detached, surgery is needed, and the outcome for regaining vision tends to depend heavily on how quickly it's treated.

The dilated exam itself is quick and painless, just some blurry near vision and light sensitivity for a few hours afterward from the drops, so there's no real downside to getting checked even if it turns out to be nothing. Retinal tears also don't always come with pain, which is part of why people sometimes wait, assuming that anything serious would hurt. A tear caught and treated with laser before the retina actually detaches is usually a same-day outpatient procedure with a fast recovery, which is a very different situation from surgery for a retina that's already come loose.

The takeaway: a few stable floaters are rarely worth worrying about, but a sudden burst of new ones along with flashes or a shadow means it's time to see an eye doctor the same day rather than waiting it out. This article is for general health information; consult a medical professional for diagnosis and treatment.
